explain.say: A lift's controller is constantly juggling calls from buttons on every floor and inside the car. Most follow a simple rule called collective control, also known as the elevator algorithm.

explain.say: The lift keeps travelling in one direction, stopping at every floor where someone wants to go that way. It passes people waiting to go the other way, and picks them up on the way back.

explain.say: When there are no more calls ahead, it turns around and serves the calls in the other direction. This stops the lift zig-zagging and makes sure nobody waits forever.

explain.say: Tall buildings put several lifts under one computer, which sends whichever car will arrive soonest. Some let you type your floor in the lobby, then group people going to nearby floors in the same car.

faq.a: It is the rule most lifts follow: keep going in one direction, stopping for everyone travelling that way, until no calls are left ahead, then reverse. Computers use the same idea to schedule reading data from disks.
asks: How does a lift decide where to go?

faq.q: Why does a lift not stop when I press the button?
faq.a: If you pressed down but the lift is going up, it passes you and picks you up on the way back down. That keeps it moving efficiently in one direction at a time.
asks: Why did the lift skip my floor?

faq.q: How do buildings with many lifts choose which one comes?
faq.a: A group controller tracks every car's position, direction and load, and gives each new call to the car expected to get there soonest.
asks: Why does a far lift come instead of the near one?

faq.a: In some buildings you enter your floor on a keypad in the lobby, and a screen tells you which lift to take. The system groups people heading to nearby floors, cutting stops and waiting time.
asks: Why do some lifts have no buttons inside?

faq.q: Does pressing the button many times make the lift come faster?
faq.a: No. The first press registers the call and extra presses do nothing. The controller already knows you are waiting.
asks: Does pressing the lift button again help?

facts: Destination dispatch systems, which group passengers by destination floor, appeared in the 1990s.
The same up-then-down rule, called the SCAN or elevator algorithm, is used to schedule reads on hard disks.

quiz.say: A lift is going up past floor 3. You are on floor 3 and pressed the down button. What happens?
quiz.show: Lift going up, you pressed down. It…

options.show: Picks you up after it finishes going up
options.say: Picks you up after it finishes going up

quiz.why: It finishes serving the upward calls, then turns around and collects you on the way down.

wrong.1: Reversing mid-trip would strand the people going up.
wrong.2: Your call is remembered and served on the way down.
